reader_question: Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?
grade_line: Documented: the atlas’s dated log, coded by the atlas
title: The atlas codes nine of the 11 state statutes in its log as moving the rules away from voters.
measure_line: Entries in the atlas’s repair log, its dated list of changes to the rules that decide who officials answer to, by how each rule changed and the direction the atlas assigns it, August 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot
notes: As of November 11, 2026: voters have cast their ballots on all three measures this chart counts as pending (repair-log entries RL62, RL63 and RL64), and none is certified. Massachusetts Question 3, for one all-candidate primary with the top two advancing, failed 61.0 percent to 39.0 in the unofficial count. Missouri Proposition A, the referendum on the 2025 congressional map, failed 61.8 percent to 38.2 in the unofficial statewide count; a no vote keeps the 2022 districts. Alaska Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal the top-four primary and ranked-choice general elections, trailed 47.4 percent to 52.6 in the unofficial count of November 10, with mailed and overseas ballots still to come. Sources: NBC Boston, Massachusetts ballot question results, November 9, 2026, a secondary source; State of Alaska, Division of Elections, 2026 General Election summary report, unofficial results, November 10, 2026; Missouri Secretary of State, unofficial statewide returns, via St. Charles County, Missouri, November 4, 2026. Retrieved November 11, 2026.

Citizen ballot initiatives: 17 entries. Seven passed, and all seven moved the rules toward voters; eight failed and left the rules in force; two are pending. A citizen initiative reaches the ballot by voters’ own petition; a referendum puts a measure the legislature passed or referred to a public vote. Three of the 10 referendums moved the rules away from voters.

State statutes: five of the nine are mid-decade congressional maps and three limit ranked-choice voting, entries the atlas says readers may weigh differently. Without those three, six of eight statutes moved the rules away from voters, still the largest share. Without the roll-up entry for 19 states, eight of 10 did.
Oath & Action grouped an agency rule, an executive action and an executive order as one instrument, and a city law with a council funding vote as another.
The atlas chose which 64 changes to record, and it records more of recent years: 33 of the 64 entries fall in 2025 and 2026.

How the atlas codes direction: Each row is coded by one of five labels. ‘Toward voters’ means the change widens who can register, vote or have a ballot counted, makes each vote weigh more equally, opens the contest that decides the seat, makes political money more limited or more visible, strengthens an independent check on officials, or adds to household security through automatic benefits. ‘Away from voters’ means the change does the reverse. ‘Voters kept existing rules’ means a ballot measure failed and the rules in force stayed, coded the same whichever way the measure would have moved power. ‘Pending’ means voters or courts have not yet decided. ‘Mixed’ means the change moved in both directions at once or left the rules in practice unchanged; the row’s own note says which. Three rules apply across parties. A partisan redraw of district maps in the middle of a decade is coded away from voters whichever party draws it and whether or not voters approved it; a court order that blocks one is coded toward voters, and one that lets it take effect is coded away. A change that widens who takes part in the deciding round (open or all-party primaries) or lets voters rank candidates is coded toward voters, and a law or amendment that bans those options is coded away; readers may weigh these entries differently, and the atlas’s profiles of those two reforms rate confidence in their effect on moderation as low.
A map redrawn in the middle of a decade counts as away from voters whichever party draws it: Texas’s HB 4 (August 2025) and California’s Proposition 50 (November 2025) both count as away.
One entry, dated March 2026, stands for all 19 state bans on ranked-choice voting; Missouri’s and Indiana’s bans also have entries of their own.
A row’s direction describes only the rule’s effect on who officials answer to.
source_line: Source: Oath & Action’s systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, repair log of 64 dated rule changes, August 6, 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot, United States: federal, state and local. Snapshot of October 15, 2026. Directions are the atlas’s own codes, set out in its coding note; each row cites its own source. One entry, New York City’s 1988 small-donor matching law, rests on a source the atlas did not check.
alt: Ranked bars of the 64 entries in the atlas’s repair log by how each rule changed, split by the atlas’s direction code. Ballot initiatives lead with 17 entries, none away from voters; court rulings follow with 14; and nine of the 11 state statutes moved the rules away from voters.
